title: Leader Election
summary:
Leader election **picks exactly one node** to do a job that must not run twice at once: accept writes for a shard, run the scheduler, own a partition. The goal is simple; the danger is **two leaders at once (split brain)**.

Ways to elect:

- **Built into [consensus](#/sd/f/consensus):** [Raft](#/sd/f/raft) elects via majority votes and numbered terms. Strongest, and what you get from etcd or ZooKeeper.
- **Lock or lease on a coordinator:** every candidate tries a conditional write (create key if absent, compare-and-set a row) with a TTL; the winner is leader and must renew. It is a [lease](#/sd/f/lease), so ownership moves when the leader stops renewing.
- **ID-based schemes** ("lowest reachable id wins"): easy, but they break under partitions because two groups each elect their own.

Whatever the mechanism, **a deposed leader may not know it yet** (GC pause, slow network). Safety comes from a [fencing token](#/sd/f/fencing-token) (the term or lease epoch) checked by the resource on every write, not from the leader's belief.

Election time is not free: failure detection plus the lease or timeout, during which there is **no leader**. Randomize timeouts so candidates don't split votes, and keep the lease long enough to ride out blips but short enough to bound downtime.

Don't elect if you can **partition the work** instead: assigning each shard to a fixed owner via [consistent hashing](#/sd/f/consistent-hashing) avoids a single hot leader. See [leader-based failover](#/sd/f/leader-based-failover).

drills.q: A scheduler leader holds a 15 s lease in a coordination service and renews every 5 s. A 20 s garbage-collection pause freezes it. What can go wrong when it wakes up?
options: Another node acquired leadership during the pause, and the old leader may still act as leader until it learns its lease expired
Nothing: a paused process cannot lose a lease
The coordination service pauses with it, so the lease is extended
The cluster has no leader forever
drills.explain: The lease expired at 15 s and a standby took over, but the paused process still believes it leads. Without a fencing token checked by the resources it writes to, both can act. Lease expiry gives liveness, not safety.

drills.q: Why do Raft-style systems randomize the election timeout?
options: So that followers rarely become candidates at the same moment and split the vote
To make elections slower and reduce load
So the oldest node always wins
To prevent heartbeats from being sent
drills.explain: If every follower had the same timeout, they would all start elections together and split the votes, forever. Randomness lets one candidate get ahead and win before the others time out.

drills.q: Leader lease TTL is 15 s, renewed every 5 s. The leader crashes right after a renewal. Standbys try to acquire the lease once every 2 s, at arbitrary phase. Taking acquisition time as negligible, what is the worst-case time until a new leader is in place, in seconds?
drills.explain: The lease cannot be taken until the full 15 s after the last renewal, and in the worst case a standby has just polled, so the next attempt comes 2 s later: 15 + 2 = 17 s. A shorter TTL or poll interval trades faster failover for more false failovers.

drills.q: Which designs elect a leader safely under network partitions? Select all that apply.
options: Nodes vote and a candidate needs a majority
Candidates race for a compare-and-set on a key in a consensus-backed store, with a TTL
Each node declares itself leader if it cannot reach any node with a lower id
Each node picks itself leader when its local clock shows the earliest start time
drills.explain: Majority voting and CAS in a consensus store both guarantee at most one winner at a time. Id- or clock-based self-declaration lets each side of a partition elect its own leader.

drills.q: Put a lease-based leader election and failover in order.
items: Candidates attempt a conditional write on the leader key; exactly one succeeds and receives a token
The winner acts as leader and renews its lease periodically
The leader crashes or is partitioned and stops renewing
The lease expires and the key becomes free
Another candidate wins the next race with a higher token
drills.explain: The higher token on the new leader is what lets resources reject any late writes from the old one.

drills.q: When should you not elect a single leader, and what do you do instead?
drills.answer: When the work can be split into independent pieces. A single leader is a throughput and availability bottleneck and an election is downtime. Partition the work (shards, hash buckets, consistent hashing) so each piece has its own owner, and elect only where something genuinely must be done by exactly one node, such as metadata or a global scheduler.
